title: Digital Regions Summit: shape the future of digital devolution
authors: Inga Newman, Engagement Delivery Manager, Government Digital Service

content.content: The government’s devolution agenda offers an opportunity to reshape how public services are delivered, enabling places to respond to local priorities and improve outcomes for their communities.

Across the country, local authorities, strategic authorities and central government teams are already using digital, data and AI to redesign services, strengthen decision-making and address complex challenges.

The opportunity now is to build on that work, connect what is already working and create the conditions for greater impact at scale. This will require sustained collaboration across local, regional and central government, combining local knowledge with shared digital, data and AI capabilities.
About the Digital Regions Summit
The Digital Regions Summit will bring together local government, strategic authorities, central government and sector partners to shape what digital devolution should look like in practice.

Designed around dialogue and collaboration, the summit will give participants an opportunity to share their perspectives, challenge assumptions and explore new ways of working across government. It will combine keynote and panel sessions with practical workshops, roundtables and problem-solving sessions.

title: Seafarers' Forum: listening to those who work at sea

content.content: On Thursday 12 November, seafarers joined colleagues from the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) at Spring Place for the Seafarers' Forum. The aim was to hear first-hand about the challenges and opportunities of working at sea and to strengthen our links with the maritime sector.
The day brought together seafarers, cadets and MCA colleagues for open discussions and workshops. Topics ranged from training and certification to wellbeing and new technology.

Ajit Jacob, Chief Examiner and Deputy Director for Seafarer Standards and Ship Registration, opened the day by explaining payment in lieu of training and cadet training. Richard Bell, Assistant Director for Marine Safety and Positioning, Navigation and Timing Services, spoke about navigational safety.

Shajan Lukose, Head of Nautical Examiners, and Sivakumar Thevaruvattath, Head of Engineer Examiners, explained how maritime training and assessment are changing. The modernised curriculum began in September 2025. It aims to match college examinations to the work seafarers do on board.
Jonathan Slater, Assistant Director of the UK Maritime Innovation Hub, presented the Hub's work on decarbonisation, digitalisation, artificial intelligence, cyber security and nuclear propulsion.
Shajan commented:
What we heard
The strongest message was the value of listening. Seafarers gave us practical insight into modern maritime careers.

Wellbeing came up repeatedly. Seafarers spoke openly about how long periods away from home affect their mental health and family life. They also talked about welfare, working conditions and keeping in touch with family.
Seafarers also shared their experiences of training, applications and digital tools. Despite the challenges, many spoke with pride about their profession and the rewards of a career at sea.
Feedback on the event echoed the positivity:
What happens next
We are reviewing the feedback from the workshops and group discussions. The forum is intended to be an annual event, with online sessions in between.

description: Seafarers joined Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) colleagues to discuss the current challenges and opportunities that working at sea can bring.

title: Five years of FiPL: delivering for farmers, nature and communities
categories: Payments to support National Parks, National Landscapes and the Broads

content.content: 2026 marks 5 years since the Farming in Protected Landscapes (FiPL) programme launched. Since it launched in 2021, FiPL has supported farmers and land managers to deliver projects that help these special places thrive.

Projects contribute to four themes: climate, nature, people and place. Together, FiPL projects have covered 1.3 million hectares, supported 11,500 educational visits, protected 274 heritage assets, and planted 410km of hedgerow and over 310,000 trees. Roughly 1,000 projects have protected or improved rivers, streams and other water bodies.

Originally planned as a 3-year programme, FiPL will now run until March 2029. If you’re farming in a Protected Landscape, you can apply for funding through your local protected landscape body. Details of what you need to know before you apply can be found on GOV.UK.

Defra evaluates FiPL to understand what is working well, assess value for money, and measure the impacts of funded projects. This post shares findings from the latest evaluation report, also drawing on data from earlier reports and latest delivery statistics to March 2026.
Supporting farmers, local communities and the environment

From ancient woodlands and wildflower-rich meadows to rugged coastlines and heather moorlands, England's Protected Landscapes are made up of National Parks, National Landscapes and the Broads. They cover almost a quarter of land in England.
44 Protected Landscapes teams work with local farmers, landowners and communities to create nature-rich, inclusive, and welcoming spaces for everyone to enjoy.
Up to March 2026, FiPL had supported more than 15,000 farmers and land managers to receive funding, across more than 7,400 projects.

Action taking place across our Protected Landscapes directly benefits the local area. Projects must contribute to their Protected Landscape's Management Plan. Funding is granted at a local level, enabling projects to respond to local issues and work at farm level.

Projects also make an important contribution to national targets, including the Protected Landscapes Targets and Outcomes Framework and government’s 30by30 commitment. Through FiPL, over 1,300 hectares of wildlife rich habitat have been created or restored outside protected sites since 2023. This contributes directly to England's legally binding national target for wildlife-rich habitats, set under the Environment Act 2021.

FiPL funding boosts financial resilience and supports the diversification activities of farm businesses. In the 2025 participant survey, 59% of survey respondents reported an improvement in the economic position of their business through FiPL. This is a particularly important outcome considering one of FiPL’s aims is to support farming businesses through the agricultural transition.
Most respondents said they used local contractors for their project and felt their project contributed to a stronger local rural economy.
Growing participation & connection

Participants gave overwhelmingly positive feedback about the programme. From 2021 – 2024, 93% of scheme participants said the programme was either in line or better than their expectations. 88% said they would recommend the programme to others.

The evaluation found evidence of wider benefits for farmers, local communities and rural economies. 83% of participants said the programme contributed to an increase in mental and physical wellbeing. Many participants associated this to feeling part of a community and building networks. FiPL gives partners the opportunity to work together to deliver benefits for people, with tailored support from FiPL officers.

The latest evaluation also found that 69% of participants reported new or stronger relationships with other farmers and land managers in their Protected Landscape. This includes 42% who reported building entirely new relationships and 27% who reported stronger existing relationships.
In addition, 74% reported more engagement with their local Protected Landscape team than before the programme started.

By March 2026, the programme had supported 241 existing farm clusters and facilitation groups and helped to establish 121 new ones. Participants reported that new and stronger relationships helped them gain knowledge, skills and confidence, supporting environmental, economic and social outcomes.
One programme aim is to help Protected Landscape teams work with farmers. Another is to help farmers work with each other. The evaluation suggests the programme supports both.
Reaching new farmers
95% of FiPL officers reported that they are engaging with farmers and land managers with little or no previous experience in an Environmental Land Management (ELM), or other agri-environment scheme.

In nearly two-thirds of cases, engagement with new farmers led to an application to the programme. In other cases, FiPL officers signposted potential applicants to other schemes that were more suitable. Around 9% of participants in 2024 to 2025 were new to agri-environment schemes - in line with the first 3 years of the programme.

Some participants use the programme as a first step into Defra schemes. The evaluation found that for many, FiPL has improved farmers confidence, inspired ideas and improved the opinion of schemes and programmes.

Many participants also return to FiPL with additional projects, often building on the success of their first project. 47% of projects in 2024-2025 were delivered by participants who had previously received FiPL funding. The evaluation found that participants with more than one completed project were more likely to go on to additional schemes than those with a single project: 38% compared with 29%.
FiPL officers are key to success
The evaluation reports highlight the vital role of FiPL officers in supporting applicants and projects.

Officers can provide advice before, during and after project design and delivery. They give participants a local contact who can provide face-to-face support. Across both evaluations, 92% of participants reported feeling very or largely supported by their Protected Landscape team.

Officers also signpost participants and potential applicants to other schemes or funding. The evaluation found this is helping Protected Landscape teams build relationships with the farming sector and provide support during the agricultural transition.
Applying FiPL’s lessons

FiPL officers also monitor project progress on the ground and report on their short- and long-term impact. This strengthens Protected Landscapes teams’ capacity to collect data and map progress against their Management Plan priorities and contributions to national targets.
The level of support from FiPL officers and associated low administrative burden perceived by participants are key strengths across both evaluation reports.
Lessons we’ve learnt through the success of FiPL has helped inform the design of other schemes, including the Farmer Collaboration Fund.

The evaluation suggests more long-term certainty of funding is likely to make the programme more impactful. At the Oxford Farming Conference in January 2026, it was confirmed that FiPL was extended until March 2029, giving more certainty to farmers and partners working in Protected Landscapes.
Looking ahead
The first 5 years of the programme show how this flexible funding model can support projects to strengthen nature, local communities and farm businesses.
Visit GOV.UK to apply now, if you are farming in a Protected Landscape.
We will continue to provide updates on the FiPL scheme and share case studies through the Farming Blog. Make sure you’re subscribed so you don’t miss an update.

description: Five years on, FiPL continues to help farmers strengthen nature, support their businesses and connect with communities. Evaluation findings highlight the value of flexible funding and local support as funding continues to March 2029.

title: Bringing sustainability to life through our curriculum

content.content: At Prospect House Specialist Support Primary School in Manchester, sustainability is something every pupil can experience, explore, and take part in. As a special educational needs school, we put inclusivity at the heart of our approach, making learning practical, accessible and relevant.

From food waste and recycling to biodiversity and our sensory garden, sustainability is part of everyday learning and school life. We were delighted to have this work recognised through the DfE Sustainability Award at Education Estates 2026.
Making sustainability part of learning

Our termly ‘Eco Warriors’ theme connects environmental science, resource efficiency and the circular economy with subject knowledge and communication skills through sensory-rich lessons and vocational activities. Rather than teaching sustainability as a standalone topic, we weave it into familiar subjects.

In English, pupils develop reading, speaking and listening skills while exploring deforestation, habitat loss, and palm oil production. In mathematics, they measure and weigh food waste, count and compare recycling data, and analyse their findings. In art and design, they reuse and repurpose materials, exploring the circular economy creatively and seeing how something discarded can have a new purpose.

These lessons extend into daily routines. Monitoring menu choices and weighing leftovers help pupils understand how everyday decisions affect food waste. We compost surplus where possible, while ‘taster pots’ offer a supportive way to try new foods and discuss sustainability.
Taking our learning outdoors
Through the National Education Nature Park, we connect learning about nature and biodiversity with practical action, using curriculum-linked resources to help pupils improve their environment.

Our sensory garden, developed with RHS Bridgewater, invites exploration through textures, colours and scents. In science, growing plants, caring for our therapy pigs and observing wildlife cameras help pupils investigate food production and the needs of living things.
We are also developing our SEND Carbon Literacy programme, using practical activities, visual supports and real-life examples to make climate change and positive action accessible.
Giving our pupils a voice

Our Eco Council helps identify priorities and develop projects, including our sensory food-waste recycling pilot and sensory garden. These experiences build communication, confidence and skills for future employment, showing pupils that their ideas and actions matter.
Bringing sustainability into your own setting

Sustainability need not sit separately from the curriculum. Connecting subjects with real-world issues and adapting activities to pupils’ needs gives everyone meaningful ways to participate. Teachers can start with one existing lesson; school leaders can build on activities already happening.
Activities already happening in your curriculum can contribute to your climate action plan, covering climate education and green skills, biodiversity, adaptation and resilience, and decarbonisation.
Free support is available through DfE’s Sustainability Support Programme:
These projects work with Let’s Go Zero Climate Action Advisors to help turn sustainability ambitions into practical action across education settings.

At Prospect House, pupils’ actions and voices matter. Start with something that matters to your pupils. Choose a sustainability challenge, such as reducing food waste or improving wildlife habitats, and link it to your curriculum. Plan practical action with pupils, give them opportunities to lead and review the difference they make.

description: Prospect House Specialist Support Primary School in Manchester shares practical ways to bring sustainability to life through the curriculum.

title: Meat inspection charges: an update on temporary changes after the court judgment
authors: Dr James Cooper, Deputy Director of Food Policy

content.content: Cymraeg

Meat inspections are vital to the UK's food system. Highly trained official vets and meat hygiene inspectors check the health of each animal and make sure the meat is safe to eat. They also protect animal welfare. This work allows the UK's meat industry to sell its products at home and export them abroad.

Last year we published a blog explaining why we charge for meat inspections, who pays and why we were reviewing the discounts on those charges. Since then, there have been important developments. This blog explains what has happened and what it means in practice.
What has happened?

Meat industry representative bodies brought a judicial review against our approach to the 2025 to 2026 meat charging rate. The court found that we could not charge for some of the activities we had included, and we have applied for permission to appeal this decision.
We do not yet know whether permission will be granted. If it is granted, an outcome may not come until next year.
We must follow the judgment now. We cannot wait for the outcome of the appeal to take action. So we have put temporary charging arrangements in place.
We want to be as clear as we can be at this stage about what this means in practice, for businesses, for taxpayers, and for the vital work our official vets and meat hygiene inspectors do every day.
What does this mean for charges?
The cost to the taxpayer of delivering official controls has not changed, yet the amount we can recover has fallen. There is no new government money to cover the difference.

We have in recent years offered businesses a taxpayer-funded discount on their charges, with the smallest businesses receiving a proportionately higher discount. There is now less public money available for this discount. As well as modifying charge rates we need to adjust how we provide taxpayer-funded discounts.
This financial year 2026 to 2027, no businesses will face materially increased bills and some will face lower invoices.
How are smaller businesses protected?

As evidenced in our recent work on a reformed discount scheme, smaller abattoirs play a vital role in local food systems and face particular challenges. We aim to continue to support smaller abattoirs this year as part of our response to the judgment.
Will these new arrangements on meat charging change again or should the appeal be granted?
These are interim arrangements, put in place  because we have to comply with the judgment now, regardless of whether permission to appeal is granted.

If an appeal is granted and succeeds, charging arrangements  may change again.  We will update businesses and the public as soon as we know more, and will explain clearly what any further change means in practice.
Why is this taking  time to respond?
This is a complex issue and we wanted to make sure we got it right, including by taking proper legal and financial advice following the judgment, rather than rushing to a conclusion.
What happens now and next financial year?
We've written to every business and met with industry representatives to explain what this means for the remainder of this financial year.
We’re still working through  what the judgment means for next year’s bills. As a result of the judgment,  we cannot guarantee any discounts next year at this stage.
While we continue to aim to support smaller operators if we can,  we’re considering what this means for future discounts.  We will meet industry again soon to discuss bills for 2027 to 2028.
What happens next with the wider reform of meat charging and how will small businesses be protected in the longer term?
Our response to the judgment sits alongside wider reform of how meat inspection costs are shared between businesses and taxpayers.
We set out the proposed changes on meat charging  at the FSA Board in September. That decision now rests with ministers.
We continue to support Defra, which leads on issues affecting small abattoirs. Many of the challenges faced by smaller operators are structural and commercial rather than regulatory.
While regulation is one factor in the operating environment, we remain committed to supporting smaller businesses wherever we can.
We will keep talking to trade bodies, businesses and other stakeholders and will provide further updates as the work develops.
Dr James Cooper, Dirprwy Gyfarwyddwr Polisi Bwyd yr ASB

Mae arolygiadau cig yn hanfodol i system fwyd y DU. Mae milfeddygon swyddogol medrus iawn ac arolygwyr hylendid cig yn gwirio iechyd pob anifail ac yn sicrhau bod y cig yn ddiogel i’w fwyta. Maen nhw hefyd yn diogelu lles anifeiliaid. Mae’r gwaith hwn yn galluogi diwydiant cig y DU i werthu ei gynhyrchion gartref a’u hallforio dramor.

Y llynedd, gwnaethon ni gyhoeddi blog a oedd yn egluro pam rydyn ni’n codi tâl am arolygiadau cig, pwy sy’n talu, a pham roedden ni’n adolygu’r gostyngiadau ar y taliadau hynny. Ers hynny, mae datblygiadau pwysig wedi bod. Mae’r blog hwn yn esbonio beth sydd wedi digwydd a beth mae’n ei olygu’n ymarferol.
Beth sydd wedi digwydd?

Gwnaeth cyrff sy’n cynrychioli’r diwydiant cig ddwyn adolygiad barnwrol yn erbyn ein dull o ymdrin â’r gyfradd codi tâl ar safleoedd cig ar gyfer 2025 i 2026. Gwnaeth y llys ganfod nad oedd modd i ni godi tâl am rai o’r gweithgareddau roedden ni wedi’u cynnwys, ac rydyn ni wedi gwneud cais am ganiatâd i apelio yn erbyn y penderfyniad hwn.
Nid ydyn ni’n gwybod eto a gawn ni ganiatâd ai peidio. Os cawn ganiatâd i apelio, efallai na ddaw canlyniad tan y flwyddyn nesaf.
Rhaid i ni ddilyn y dyfarniad nawr. Allwn ni ddim aros am ganlyniad yr apêl cyn gweithredu. Felly, rydyn ni wedi rhoi trefniadau dros dro ar waith.

Hoffen ni fod mor glir â phosib ar hyn o bryd ynghylch beth mae hyn yn ei olygu’n ymarferol – i fusnesau, i drethdalwyr, ac i’r gwaith hanfodol mae ein milfeddygon swyddogol a’n harolygwyr hylendid cig yn ei wneud bob dydd.
Beth mae hyn yn ei olygu ar gyfer taliadau?
Nid yw’r gost i’r trethdalwr o gynnal rheolaethau swyddogol wedi newid, ond mae’r swm y gallwn ni ei adennill wedi gostwng. Nid yw’r llywodraeth yn rhoi arian ychwanegol i dalu’r gwahaniaeth.

Yn ystod y blynyddoedd diwethaf, rydyn ni wedi cynnig gostyngiad, a ariennir gan drethdalwyr, ar daliadau busnesau, gyda’r busnesau lleiaf yn derbyn y gostyngiad cyfrannol mwyaf. Erbyn hyn, mae llai o arian cyhoeddus ar gael ar gyfer y gostyngiad hwn.
Yn ogystal â newid cyfraddau’r taliadau, mae angen i ni addasu sut rydyn ni’n darparu gostyngiadau a ariennir gan drethdalwyr.
Y flwyddyn ariannol hon (2026/27), ni fydd unrhyw fusnesau’n wynebu biliau sy’n sylweddol uwch, a bydd rhai yn wynebu anfonebau is.
Sut mae busnesau llai yn cael eu diogelu?

Fel y gwelir yn ein gwaith diweddar ar gynllun gostyngiadau diwygiedig, mae lladd-dai llai yn chwarae rhan hanfodol mewn systemau bwyd lleol ac yn wynebu heriau penodol. Ein nod yw parhau i gefnogi lladd-dai llai eleni fel rhan o’n hymateb i’r dyfarniad.
A fydd y trefniadau newydd hyn ar godi tâl ar safleoedd cig yn newid eto pe bai’r apêl yn cael ei chaniatáu?
Trefniadau dros dro yw’r rhain sydd wedi’u rhoi ar waith oherwydd bod yn rhaid i ni gydymffurfio â’r dyfarniad nawr, ni waeth a gawn ni ganiatâd i apelio ai peidio.

Os caniateir apêl ac os bydd yn llwyddo, gallai’r trefniadau codi tâl newid eto. Byddwn ni’n rhoi’r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf i fusnesau a’r cyhoedd cyn gynted ag y byddwn ni’n gwybod mwy, a byddwn ni’n ei gwneud hi’n glir beth mae unrhyw newid pellach yn ei olygu’n ymarferol.
Pam mae’n cymryd amser i ymateb?
Mater cymhleth yw hwn, ac roedden ni am sicrhau ein bod ni’n delio ag ef yn iawn, gan gynnwys ceisio cyngor cyfreithiol ac ariannol priodol yn dilyn y dyfarniad, yn hytrach na rhuthro i gasgliad.
Beth sy’n digwydd nawr a’r flwyddyn ariannol nesaf?
Rydyn ni wedi ysgrifennu at bob busnes ac wedi cwrdd â chynrychiolwyr y diwydiant i egluro beth mae hyn yn ei olygu am weddill y flwyddyn ariannol hon.
Rydyn ni’n dal i weithio ar beth mae’r dyfarniad yn ei olygu ar gyfer biliau’r flwyddyn nesaf. O ganlyniad i’r dyfarniad, allwn ni ddim gwarantu unrhyw ostyngiadau y flwyddyn nesaf ar hyn o bryd.

Er ein bod ni’n parhau i anelu at gefnogi gweithredwyr llai os gallwn, rydyn ni’n ystyried beth mae hyn yn ei olygu ar gyfer gostyngiadau yn y dyfodol. Byddwn ni’n cwrdd â’r diwydiant eto’n fuan i drafod biliau ar gyfer 2027 i 2028.
Beth sy’n digwydd nesaf gyda’r gwaith diwygio ehangach ar godi tâl ar safleoedd cig, a sut y bydd busnesau bach yn cael eu diogelu yn yr hirdymor?
Mae ein hymateb i’r dyfarniad yn sefyll ochr yn ochr â gwaith diwygio ehangach ar sut y caiff costau arolygu cig eu rhannu rhwng busnesau a threthdalwyr.
Gwnaethon ni amlinellu’r newidiadau arfaethedig i godi tâl ar safleoedd cig yng nghyfarfod Bwrdd yr Asiantaeth Safonau Bwyd (ASB) ym mis Medi. Mae’r penderfyniad hwnnw bellach yn nwylo gweinidogion.

Rydyn ni’n parhau i gefnogi Adran yr Amgylchedd, Bwyd a Materion Gwledig (Defra), sy’n arwain ar faterion sy’n effeithio ar ladd-dai bach. Mae llawer o’r heriau sy’n wynebu gweithredwyr llai yn rhai strwythurol a masnachol yn hytrach na rheoleiddiol.
Er bod rheoleiddio’n un ffactor yn yr amgylchedd gweithredu, rydyn ni wedi ymrwymo o hyd i gefnogi busnesau llai pryd bynnag y gallwn.
Byddwn ni’n parhau i siarad â chyrff masnach, busnesau a rhanddeiliaid eraill, a byddwn ni’n darparu diweddariadau pellach wrth i’r gwaith ddatblygu.

title: Departments are still failing to meet their legal obligations to review regulations

content.content: Post-implementation reviews (PIRs) are a legal obligation to review and evaluate existing regulations and a critical part of how government demonstrates that regulations are working as intended, or identifies how they can be fixed. However, despite repeated calls over many years and firm commitments from permanent secretaries to address the problem, departments are still failing to get on top of their obligations to complete PIRs on time – four departments still have 6 PIRs outstanding: BIST, DfT, FSA and MHCLG.

In our last PIR blog in May 2026 we reported that progress had stalled, with new PIRs becoming overdue as quickly as departments were completing previous overdue ones. We said that departments needed to complete new PIRs on time as well as managing the backlog – unfortunately they have failed to do this and although there has been a small reduction (from 47 in May to 40 now) far more needs to be done.
Overdue Post-Implementation Reviews by Department
*For data from before the changes in departmental responsibilities in 2026, PIRs for former DBT, DCMS and DSIT have been assigned to current departments based on policy areas.

Post-Implementation Reviews are an important way for the Government to support its growth agenda by identifying regulations that place an excessive burden on businesses and inhibit growth. If done well they should identify opportunities to revise regulations to make them more pro-growth. Given their desire to promote economic growth as well as their legal commitments, we would have expected Government to be more focussed on completing PIRs.

The RPC has been reporting on departments' performance in undertaking PIRs and the backlog of overdue PIRs (those that have not been undertaken by the fifth anniversary of the introduction of the regulation) since the start of 2025. Departments are reminded 12 months in advance of regulations approaching their review date.
A full breakdown of overdue and upcoming PIRs by department is published on our website.
Departments' progress is set out below.
Strong performance
Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ)

•	In May we challenged DESNZ to complete all remaining PIRs by our next update. We are pleased to announce that DESNZ have done so and now have no PIRs outstanding. We hope they continue to remain on top of their commitments.
Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA)

•	In May we congratulated DEFRA on having reduced their backlog down to a single PIR. DEFRA is now up to date with all their PIRs due in 2026. We hope they continue to remain on top of their commitments.
Progress made, but more to do
Department for Transport (DfT)

•	DfT committed to completing their overdue PIRs by June 2025 - a deadline they missed.  Following my letter in December, DfT's permanent secretary wrote to me to say that the department was taking steps to accelerate clearances and recommitted to completing all outstanding PIRs by the end of March 2027.

•	Of the 9 PIRs overdue in May 26, 7 have now been completed, and we have been told that one more is awaiting clearance. However, 4 new measures have become overdue since May, leaving a total of 6 overdue measures. All 4 of the new measures have been reviewed by the RPC and are awaiting publication. DfT have done a good job in reducing their backlog and are on track to meet their new commitment.  We expect them to keep on top of their statutory deadlines on new PIRs going forward.
HM Treasury (HMT)

•	HMT previously committed to completing all overdue PIR’s ‘in due course’. In May we identified 3 overdue PIRs. It has since been confirmed that one of these is reviewed annually by the Financial Policy Committee and another has been completed, leaving only 1 legacy PIR overdue. HMT have informed us this is currently being drafted. One additional PIR has become overdue since May. HMT have informed us that they intend to complete this as part of a wider review of the Financial Services and Markets Act next year. HMT have reduced their backlog and have plans for completing all outstanding PIRs. We expect them to keep on top of their statutory deadlines on new PIRs going forward.
Progress stalled
Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC)

•	Last year, DHSC committed to completing their overdue PIRs as soon as possible. After some improvement in the first half of the year, there has been no further progress and 3 PIRs remain overdue. DHSC need to do more and I will write to their permanent secretary to chase progress.
Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS)

•	DCMS was formed in Summer 2026 from DCMS and parts of DSIT. The new department has 3 PIRs overdue. The former DCMS had no overdue PIRs, while DSIT had committed to clear all of their overdue PIRs by April.

•	After progress by former DSIT earlier in the year, this is a disappointing result. We expect DCMS to complete the remaining PIRs by our next update; I will write to their permanent secretary to remind them of their statutory obligations.
Disappointing Performance
Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST)

•	BIST was formed in Summer 2026 from DBT and parts of DSIT. The new department has 6 overdue PIRs - the joint highest number of any department. DSIT and DBT had both committed to clear all of their overdue PIRs by April.

•	The former DBT has cleared all legacy PIRs, however, the department is not keeping up with new commitments, with 4 PIRs outstanding, all of which became overdue in the last year. Both former DSIT PIRs are still overdue from our previous update.

•	The Department have informed us that 4 of the 6 overdue PIRs are currently undergoing clearances. I will write to the department’s permanent secretary to remind them of their legal obligations and say that we expect to see significant progress by our next update.
Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG)
•	MHCLG committed to completing all their backlog by November 2026, however, they still have 6 PIRs outstanding, the same number as in May and the joint highest number of any department.

•	The Permanent Secretary wrote to me earlier this month acknowledging that their performance has fallen short of their commitment set out in the Spring. His letter set out the progress the Department is making, with 5 of the outstanding PIRs expected to be completed in November and the sixth in February 2027. I look forward to seeing all of MHCLGs outstanding PIRs being completed by our next update.
Food Standards Agency (FSA)
•	In May 2026 the FSA had 6 PIRs overdue and they have made no progress in reducing this number leaving them with the joint highest number of any department.

title: Summer 2026: a record year for heat-related deaths in a changing UK climate

content.content: The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has published an interim assessment of heat-associated mortality during summer 2026. We estimate that 5,258 deaths were associated with heat across 7 heat episodes between May and August, the highest annual total recorded since we first published heat mortality reports.

These findings provide an early indication of the health impacts of this summer's heat. However, they are not the final figures. The analysis is based on provisional mortality data and the final number will be published in the annual official statistics report in early 2027.
What does this report cover?

The report estimates the total number of deaths associated with specific periods of hot weather. It looks at what was observed during heat episodes by comparing mortality during those periods with non-heat periods around the same time.

This interim publication focuses on the overall mortality impact of summer 2026. It does not yet include the detailed analyses by age, geography or cause of death that will be available in the final report. It also does not include comparisons between the deaths observed this summer and the number we might have expected based on longer-term modelling. Those analyses require more complete mortality data and will be included in the annual publication.
What can we say about summer 2026?
The headline finding is clear. Summer 2026 was exceptional.
There were 7 heat episodes between May and August, covering a total of 41 days. This is the greatest number of heat episode days recorded since we began producing these analyses in 2016.

The largest proportion of impacts were seen during the early heat events. The May and June heat episodes accounted for more than 3,000 heat-associated deaths, with the June episode alone associated with an estimated 2,401 deaths. Together, the first 2 episodes were associated with more heat-related mortality than all of the following heat episodes combined.

However, substantial impacts were observed across the other heat episodes throughout the summer. The heat episodes in July and August were collectively associated with more than 2,000 heat-associated deaths, demonstrating that the health risks from heat were not limited to a single extreme event but lasted through multiple periods of hot weather across both spring and summer.

The timing of the heat events is also worth noting. The first heat episode occurred in late May, before many people would traditionally think of heat as a significant health risk. That early-season impact is consistent with evidence that unusually hot weather can be particularly harmful when it occurs before people have had an opportunity to adjust and prepare.

Taken together, these findings suggest that preparedness cannot focus solely on a small number of exceptionally hot days. In 2026, hot weather was a recurring feature of the summer, highlighting the importance of embedding heat-health actions into routine activities across the season, rather than relying solely on short-term responses to individual heat events.

At the same time, it is important not to over-interpret these findings in isolation. The annual report, due in early 2027, will allow us to place what we see in a wider historical context and assess how it compares with what might have been expected based on previous relationship between temperature and mortality.
Was this expected, and what does this mean for the future?
While the mortality estimate is unprecedented, the broader picture is not surprising.

Summer 2026 included an unusually high number of heat episodes, several periods of sustained hot weather, and significant events occurring early in the season. England's population is also ageing, with more people living with health conditions sensitive to heat, increasing the number of people potentially vulnerable to the health effects of extreme heat.
Together, these factors mean that larger health impacts from heat are becoming increasingly likely, despite increasing levels of action and awareness of the risks associated with high temperatures.

For many years, the focus of planning has naturally fallen on the hottest periods of summer. But the largest impacts this year occurred much earlier. If heat events continue to occur in May and early June, preparedness activities need to be in place before then.
More broadly, heat can no longer be viewed as an occasional hazard. Climate change is increasing the frequency, intensity and duration of hot weather, and the risks to health are growing as a result.

Alerts, public health advice and emergency response will always remain vitally important. But they are only part of the answer. Reducing future impacts will increasingly depend on longer-term adaptation across health and care services, housing, the built environment and local communities.
The climate is changing rapidly. The challenge now is to make sure we can prepare and adapt at the same rate.

title: Product management is about decisions, not just delivery

content.content: What does good product management look like when the answer isn’t always to build another product?

Like many organisations with an established digital estate, the Department for Education increasingly works across existing services, platforms, policies, data and organisational boundaries. Problems do not always fit neatly inside one product or one team.
At a recent product management community away day, we explored what that means for our practice. We talked about decisions, evidence, user journeys, reuse and roadmaps. One key idea came through:
Product management creates value through the quality of the decisions we help an organisation make, not just the things we deliver.
Start with the outcome

Product managers do not simply help organisations deliver things. We help make choices about which problems deserve attention, which outcomes we’re trying to change, what evidence we have, what we’re assuming and, sometimes, whether we should build something at all.

Those questions become increasingly important when we’re not working from a blank sheet of paper. A decision about one service can affect another. Building something new creates something else to operate and maintain. Improving one part of a journey doesn’t necessarily improve the journey as a whole.
That’s also why I think we need to be careful about how we use roadmaps.

Delivery plans matter. Teams need to understand commitments, dependencies and dates. But a roadmap shouldn’t just tell us what we’re going to build. It should make visible what we’re trying to change, why we believe something will make a difference, what evidence and assumptions sit behind that belief, and what would cause us to change course.
Delivering everything on a roadmap isn’t success if the outcome doesn’t follow.
A roadmap should help us make and revisit choices, not turn an earlier assumption into a promise we feel compelled to defend.
Ask what would make you change your mind
Making better decisions means being prepared to challenge them.
What outcome are we trying to change? What evidence do we have? What are we assuming? Why this solution and why now? What happens if we do nothing?
And one question I particularly want us to get comfortable asking:
What evidence would make us change our minds?
The point is not to slow decisions down. It’s to make the reasoning behind them clearer.
Testing isn’t about proving that our original idea was right. It’s about reducing uncertainty and helping us make the next decision better.
But there is another side to this. It is not enough simply to tell product managers to challenge.
If we expect people to surface uncertainty, question established plans and make difficult trade-offs visible, leaders need to create an environment where they can do that constructively.
We cannot ask people to exercise judgement while making thoughtful challenge professionally risky.
Is this decision a hat, a haircut or a tattoo?
Not every decision needs the same amount of scrutiny.
One analogy we used was hats, haircuts and tattoos.
Some decisions are like hats. They’re cheap and easily reversible. Try one, learn something and take it off if it doesn’t work.
Others are more like haircuts. A poor choice is recoverable, but it can take a little time.
And some decisions resemble tattoos. They’re consequential, expensive or difficult to reverse.
The analogy is deliberately light-hearted, but the principle matters: the evidence and challenge should reflect the consequence and reversibility of the decision.

A small, reversible experiment shouldn’t necessarily require months of discovery. Equally, we shouldn’t make an expensive commitment affecting several services, with tattoo-level consequences, on hat-level evidence.
We’re not looking for perfect certainty. We’re trying to make thoughtful decisions with the evidence available and be clear about what would make us continue, change direction or stop.
Users experience journeys, not organisational structures
We explored another part of this by deliberately stepping outside government services.
We looked at what should have been a straightforward journey across London using shared transport.

Availability, reservations, changing transport, geofencing, parking, mobile connectivity and a diminishing phone battery all came into play. Each part of the experience could be explained individually. Together, the traveller missed the train. The traveller had a journey problem.
That matters for government services too.
Users do not necessarily know which team, service or directorate is responsible for each part of a journey, nor should they need to.
Each team can make a perfectly rational decision within its own boundary and, collectively, we can still create a poor experience for the user.

It means product managers need to look beyond their own product. What happens before it? What happens afterwards? Which outcomes do we share with other teams? What capability, research, data or learning could we reuse rather than create again?

And no single profession owns the user’s voice. Researchers, designers, technologists, analysts, delivery professionals, policy colleagues and operational teams encounter different evidence and different parts of the problem.
Better decisions happen when those perspectives come together around the outcome.
Prioritisation is a decision too
There’s another condition for good product management that’s easy to overlook: organisations need to make choices.
Lots of things can be important at the same time. But prioritisation isn’t simply recognising that they’re important.
Prioritisation means deciding what won’t happen, or at least what won’t happen yet.
When competing priorities aren’t resolved, the trade-off doesn’t disappear. It can simply move further down the organisation to teams that don’t have the authority to resolve it.
Product managers have a role here. We can make trade-offs visible, bring evidence, explain opportunity cost and show what another commitment means for existing outcomes.
But product management cannot substitute for organisational prioritisation.
Better decisions need to happen at the right level, with the people who have the authority and evidence to make them.
Challenge. Decide. Learn.
For me, much of this comes back to three words we used during the day:
Challenge the assumption. Be clear about the outcome, what we know, what we’re assuming and what would make us change our minds.
Decide using the evidence available. Make the trade-offs visible and don’t wait for certainty that may never come.
Learn from what happens. Measure whether the outcome changed, not simply whether we delivered the feature, and be willing to change course.
The model we explored was deliberately simple:
Outcome → Hypothesis → Evidence → Decision → Learning
None of that happens particularly well in isolation.

It relies on product, design, research, technology, delivery, data, policy and operations bringing different perspectives and evidence. It relies on leaders making choices and creating the conditions for thoughtful challenge. And it relies on teams actively looking beyond their own boundaries.
Processes, standards and governance can support that, but relationships matter too. We need to create the space for someone to say:
“I’m not convinced this is the right thing to do. Can we look at the evidence again?”
Product management isn’t simply about making a roadmap happen.
At its best, it’s about helping an organisation make better decisions about outcomes, together.

description: Debbie Blanchard reflects on how product managers can use evidence, challenge and prioritisation to make better decisions about outcomes, not just delivery.

title: Life as a Marine Officer: no two days are the same

content.content: From inspecting fishing vessels and visiting fish markets to advising coastal communities, Marine Officers at the Marine Management Organisation (MMO) have a varied role supporting our marine environment and fishing industry.
We spoke to four Marine Officers about what brought them to the role and what they enjoy about their work.
Different routes into the role
There is no single route to becoming a Marine Officer.
Wendy already worked for the MMO as a fishing vessel licensing officer when she decided to broaden her skills and experience.
“I saw becoming a Marine Officer as an opportunity to broaden my skills, learn more about the UK fishing industry and work directly with local stakeholders,” she said.
Samuel, based in Plymouth, joined after working on EU-funded marine projects, while Rhiannon, based in North Shields, first experienced the MMO during a university placement.
Paul made a bigger career change, joining after 20 years in sales and business development and bringing transferable skills including communication and experience working with people.
Their experiences show the different backgrounds and skills people can bring to the role.
No two days are the same
The work can include inspecting fishing vessels, measuring fishing gear, carrying out market checks and helping fishers understand regulations.
Rhiannon said: “One day you could be measuring fishing nets, inspecting a restaurant, attending a wildlife event, writing a consultation response or inspecting a dredger.
“I really enjoy being out and about and having an active role rather than knowing that every working day will look the same.”
Fishing is a 24-hour industry too. Wendy recalls carrying out fish market inspections at 5am, while some Marine Officers have opportunities to work at sea.
For Rhiannon, being a seagoing Boarding Officer is a highlight: “It gives you a real understanding of the industry you’re working with and regulating.”
Working directly with fishers has given Rhiannon a greater understanding of the realities of the industry.
“Fishing can be incredibly demanding. It’s physical, dangerous and can mean spending long periods away from home.

“Working directly with fishers has allowed me to see the realities of the job first-hand, and I think that understanding this is really important when your role involves both supporting the industry and ensuring compliance.”
Building relationships is an important part of that.
“You become a familiar face within your local fishing industry. People will come to you with questions, tell you what’s happening locally and ask for advice.”
Developing your skills
Marine Officers receive training and support to develop the specialist knowledge and practical skills they need, from fisheries and legislation to different fishing methods and compliance.
For Wendy, one of the most important lessons has been not to be afraid to ask questions.
“There is always someone in the MMO who can provide you with a steer, advice and experience to support you.”
Rhiannon agrees: “That variety means you’re continually learning, even once you've been in the role for a while.”
Thinking about becoming a Marine Officer?
The four officers highlighted similar qualities for the role: being willing to learn, working well with others, having good attention to detail and being comfortable adapting to different situations.

Wendy says that while experience in marine studies or fisheries can be useful, it is not essential as training is provided. Being enthusiastic about learning, flexible and willing to work outdoors throughout the year are just as important.

Samuel’s advice is not to be put off by the learning curve: “Take your time, speak to your trainer or line manager, and don’t be afraid to ask for help. With each day you are building more confidence in your abilities, skills and knowledge.”

Rhiannon’s advice is simple: “If you enjoy being out and about, have good attention to detail, are personable and are comfortable dealing with situations that can sometimes be challenging, put yourself forward.”

And Paul’s is even shorter: “Do it! I was quite nervous when I joined the MMO, but the training, support and mentoring is excellent.”Interested in becoming a Marine Officer? Find out more about our current opportunities and how to apply.

title: Enabling estate agents to speed up transactions
authors: Mike Pomeroy, General Manager at HIPLA

content.content: Key takeaways

HIPLA joined the Geovation Accelerator Programme in 2018. The programme, backed by HM Land Registry and Ordnance Survey, provides geospatial and PropTech start-ups with grant funding and 12 months of support, encouraging the innovative use of our data to benefit the property market, society and the economy.

Hello, I'm Mike Pomeroy, General Manager at HIPLA. We help estate agents onboard clients at the start of a sale, with ID and anti-money laundering (AML) checks done and the legal information gathered upfront so the conveyancer can start on day one.
Founded in 2016, we're a fully remote team of 11 and the sole supplier of ID and AML checks to Propertymark Company Advantage, supporting more than 2,000 agency branches and over 2,000 conveyancers.
Why we built it

HIPLA began with one problem: fall-throughs, which happen in around a third of transactions. Our earliest work, binding reservation agreements with Mishcon de Reya, was intended to give buyers and sellers a real commitment at the point of offer. During this work, we noticed that transactions fell apart because they were slow, and they were slow because the essential work started too late. So, in 2020 we pivoted to sorting compliance and legal information at the front door.
What we do
Our platform supplies five products so they appear as the agent's own:

The Digital Legal Pack is the product we're proudest of – gathering the material information, title data and seller forms upfront means that the buyer's conveyancer receives a ready-to-go pack on day one rather than a stack of enquiries on day 40. With the government's reform roadmap pointing towards upfront information as standard, this is moving from nice-to-have to expected.
Customer feedback
Our customers are seeing the benefits of getting sellers transaction-ready earlier:
Geovation
We joined the Geovation Accelerator Programme in 2018. The £20,000 grant covered early set-up costs, and Geovation's engineers gave us design guidance while we were still working out what to build.

The bigger value was the doors it opened. Presenting to the HM Land Registry Board led to an introduction to Propertymark that grew into our Company Advantage partnership; Kate Faulkner OBE and the Home Buying and Selling Council helped shape our early Digital Legal Pack; and several of our first clients came from Propertymark training days at the Geovation hub.
How we use HM Land Registry data

At the heart of the Digital Legal Pack sits HMLR data, drawn directly from HMLR's Business Gateway which gives businesses direct access to official property information. The moment our users confirm an address, we find its title number and one click brings in official copies of the register and title plan, plus any lease or deed the register refers to. We check the registered owners against the people selling, and we lay HMLR's INSPIRE index polygons, (the mapped extent of every registered freehold), over the plot as Ordnance Survey maps it. So, a strip of garden the title doesn't include is a question for the seller before marketing, not a surprise at exchange.
What's next

Soon we’ll be adding automated title analysis that explains register entries in plain English and flags information needing attention. It describes rather than advises, but it gives an agent the material information they must disclose on day one.  Ordnance Survey data will link the analysis to the correct property using unique property reference numbers, and the OS National Geographic database allows title boundaries to be compared with mapped plots and buildings.

When our rebuilt platform launches in the next few weeks, automated title analysis will be built in, the most complete compliance toolkit we have ever created, providing new ways for the agents we work with to earn from the work they already do.

title: CMA statement on UK launch of Meta Muse

content.content: The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has been clear that UK consumer protection law applies to AI products. This includes personal AI agents like Meta’s Muse, which has been launched in the UK today. Similar products are likely to be introduced in the UK in the coming months. AI offerings continue to develop rapidly with new services or tools quickly becoming available for consumers and for businesses.

Personal AI agents could offer significant benefits to consumers, saving people time, helping them to organise tasks, and access other products or services more easily. This statement is focused on consumer protection, which the CMA enforces, but the introduction of personal AI agents also has implications for other regulatory regimes, including data protection and financial services. We have been working closely with the Information Commission (ICO), the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) and Ofcom as members of the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF) in anticipation of the launch of these products in the UK. The DRCF published a joint letter to Ministers on Monday 16 November about the responsible development of personal AI agents in the UK.

While the technology and capabilities becoming available are new, as we explained in our guidance on AI agents earlier this year, the same consumer protection rules apply to these new products and technologies as to any other product or service.

Consumer protection laws require businesses to treat people fairly, to protect their customers’ interests appropriately, and to operate in good faith. That means that what a consumer is told about a product when purchasing, signing up for and using it must be clear and must not be misleading or omit key information. The terms and conditions must be fair.

When applied to agentic technology, these principles are of the utmost importance. These are products with the potential to transform markets and the relationships that people have with businesses, but they are also very new. Customers may not have used similar products before. The suppliers of agentic products will always have far more information than their customers do about how the product works, its limitations and the risks that may arise when using it. It is the responsibility of these suppliers to understand and act on those risks. They must put the safety, security and interests of their customers at the heart of design on an ongoing basis.
What does this mean in practice for AI agents?

It is important that the way a personal AI agent is presented to consumers is consistent with how it operates in practice. When people are purchasing or signing up to use an AI agent the supplier should make them aware of the risks or limitations of the agent. When people are using the agent, they need to know the right information at the right time to allow them to take informed decisions about how they use the agent. This includes information that allows them to understand the potential implications of giving the agent different levels of access to their information or autonomy to act on their behalf. Consumers need to have the ability easily to exercise control when using the agent, and to be made aware of how to make choices and what effect those choices will have on the agent’s actions.

In addition to being clear, the way the agent is presented to the consumer, and the way it interacts with the consumer in practice, should be consistent with the terms and conditions that apply to the consumer’s use of the agent. Terms and conditions should be consistent with the marketing and sales claims and should not contain surprises for the consumer about where responsibility lies if something goes wrong.

Companies that are planning to offer new products to consumers in the UK are responsible for ensuring that the way they offer those products is compliant with UK consumer protection rules. We recognise that this technology is developing quickly. In that context, we are happy to engage with businesses who are planning to introduce these products as those businesses take steps to ensure they comply with UK laws.
Our engagement with Meta

Over the past several weeks, since Meta informed us of their plans to launch in the UK, we have engaged with them on the importance of ensuring consumers’ statutory rights are reflected in their terms and conditions, and of offering Muse to UK consumers in a way that complies with the requirements of consumer law. Following our engagement, Meta has made changes to their terms and conditions to make them fairer for consumers. We remain in ongoing discussions with Meta. As Muse is rolled out in the UK we will continue to engage with Meta and will be closely reviewing how Muse is presented and functions in practice. If we have concerns, we will not hesitate to act to protect UK consumers. We will also continue to co-ordinate closely with other regulators in the DRCF as they engage with Meta on similar issues.
Our message to consumers

Suppliers are responsible for ensuring that they provide consumers with the information they need to assess limitations and risks when deciding to use a personal AI assistant – both when they initially sign up and when using the agent. They must also ensure that consumers can easily control what the AI assistant accesses and its level of autonomy. These are, however, new technologies that most of us will not have used before and that are continuing to develop.

In that context, we would encourage customers to consider carefully not only the information presented to them about the potential benefits of an AI agent, but also the information presented to them about risks and limitations. While the agent may be designed to work on its own, customers might want to think about how clearly they understand what that means in practice, and how much autonomy they want to give the agent. We strongly encourage customers to check their settings when signing up to use an agent and regularly after that to ensure that the permissions and approvals are set appropriately according to the risks the customer is prepared to accept. Some people may decide to start slowly and build up their usage over time as they become more familiar with how the agent works.

Together with the other DRCF regulators we want to hear if customers face challenges relating to consumer protection, privacy and data protection, or payments and financial services when using AI agents. To help customers to share that information, we have set up a form that customers can use to share their experience of using Muse or other AI agents. Share your views on personal AI agents.
Joint tips from the CMA and ICO

Data protection and consumer rights closely overlap where AI is concerned, so the Competition and Markets Authority and ICO have joined forces to recommend the following steps for anyone thinking about using an AI agent or chatbot.
Consider the pros and cons: Weigh up the potential benefits and risks of using an AI agent, especially as agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously.

Check how much the agent can do without asking you: Look for settings that control when the agent needs your approval and remember you can start with the most limited mode. Look for an explanation of what information or tools the agent wants to access, and if permission is for a one off task, or ongoing.
Know what the AI agent can access and what permissions it has: Understand your settings when signing up and check back in regularly to ensure the permissions and approvals are still right for you.
When it comes to your data

Check the privacy controls and default settings: Look at the privacy and data sharing settings available, including whether your information can be used to train AI or personalise content or advertising. Check what information the organisation says it will use, how it will be used, and what controls you have over this.
Start with limited access: You don’t have to connect every account or application the agent or platform suggests. Remember you can manage your access permissions on an ongoing basis.

Look for controls over what the agent remembers: Make sure you understand what information may be stored or retained. If the service offers memory, get familiar with how you can switch off, edit or delete saved information.
Think carefully about the personal information you directly share or allow the agent to access: including sensitive information about yourself and information about other people.

title: The Civil Service STEM Challenge continues to inspire secondary-school students to get involved in policymaking as it moves into its 5th year

title: Misleading reporting on Renters’ Deposits

content.content: A number of media articles cover the government’s plans to retain interest raised on renters' deposits along with misleading claims.
These claims have misrepresented the intention of secondary legislation currently being considered by Parliament, and ministers' policy intentions for Tenancy Deposit Protection.
The Government is driving up conditions for tenants in the private rented sector and improving how tenancy deposit schemes work is one of the ways we are delivering on this commitment.

The planned change will mean more of the interest raised from tenants' deposits could benefit tenants themselves, by enabling interest to be spent on Government programmes, instead of being kept as profit by the companies running the schemes.
This will mean better value for both tenants and taxpayers.
For any money received, the Government will publish the amounts, the programme(s) funded, and any metrics demonstrating the value delivered.
An MHCLG spokesperson said:
“We don’t accept these claims - the Tenancy Deposit Schemes do not enable the Government to profit from tenants’ deposits.
"These changes will enable more of the interest raised from tenants' deposits to benefit tenants themselves, instead of being kept as profit by the companies running the schemes"

title: Beyond knowledge: what dairy farmers can teach us about behaviour change in antibiotic stewardship

content.content: This week is World Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Awareness Week and the perfect opportunity to hear from one of the scholars participating in the VMD-University of Zambia postgraduate programme, Inyambo Mumbula. Funded by the Fleming Fund and supported by technical expertise from VMD, his research focuses on antimicrobial resistance in Zambia, centred around smallholder dairy farmers. In this blog, Inyambo brings to life how his research has put farmers at the centre of improving antimicrobial stewardship.
What can a smallholder dairy farmer teach an environmental safety officer, a social policy expert or a digital health specialist about behaviour change?
More than we might expect.

Over the last three years, my research has explored the knowledge, attitudes and practices of smallholder dairy farmers in Zambia regarding the use of antimicrobials. Smallholder dairy farmers manage relatively small herds of non-native breeds such as Friesian or Jersey cows, or local breeds which produce low milk yields primarily for household consumption or local market sales.

My research identified gaps in knowledge and practices around the responsible use of antimicrobials, with potential implications for the development of AMR. In response, I employed a Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) approach to develop a radio- and text message-based intervention designed to reach smallholder farmers and support better antimicrobial stewardship.
Putting antibiotic stewardship on the airwaves

The resulting intervention used a radio drama, interactive radio discussions and text messages to communicate good antimicrobial stewardship practices in an accessible and locally relevant way. Rather than relying solely on technical information, the radio content placed decisions about antimicrobial use within situations farmers could recognise from everyday life. Text messages complemented the radio programmes by providing reminders and reinforcing important behaviours between episodes. The intervention was developed with farmers using Human-Centred Design, so their perspectives helped shape not only what was communicated, but how it was communicated.
Taking the lessons to UNICEF

On 11–12 June 2026, I joined a UNICEF learning event on Social and Behaviour Change, focused on how we can better listen to communities and co-design interventions with them. The diversity in the room included government ministries, United Nations agencies, civil society organisations, SBC practitioners and digital institutions working across health, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), social policy and community development. This diversity reinforced an important message: SBC is not confined to one sector or discipline.
During the meeting, I shared insights from my PhD research. Three lessons stood out:

One of the issues I explored was adherence to antimicrobial withdrawal periods. This is the length of time that must lapse between the final administration of the medicine and the point that the treated animal can be slaughtered to enter the food chain or when produce, such as milk, can be taken from the treated animal. Withdrawal periods exist to ensure the medicinal substances have been adequately metabolised or excreted. On paper, the solution can appear straightforward: educate farmers about withdrawal periods, explain the risks of antimicrobial residues in animal products, and reinforce the rules with regulatory actions and sanctions. But listening to farmers revealed a much more complex reality.

Some farmers knew about antimicrobial withdrawal periods yet chose not to comply with them. For instance, milk was sold through informal markets, processed or allowed to sour, while some believed that boiling could make the milk safe. These practices were often responses to livelihood pressures, household needs, market demands and limited access to veterinary support and advice, rather than necessarily evidence of ignorance or disregard for regulations.  This was an important reminder that knowledge alone may not be enough to support good practices and the threat of sanctions does not automatically produce sustained behaviour change. People make decisions within real-life circumstances. For SBC practitioners and those of us invested in promoting antimicrobial stewardship, this means that asking “What don’t people know?” may not be enough. We also need to ask: “What circumstances make this behaviour difficult, and what are people trying to achieve through it?”
A second lesson was about the role of radio and text messaging.

In an era where Mobile Health - the practice of medicine and public health supported by mobile and wireless devices - is often associated with sophisticated mobile applications, digital platforms and smartphones, it can be tempting to assume that newer technology automatically means better interventions.
My research suggested otherwise for many smallholder farmers in rural areas.

Radio remains an important and trusted source of information, particularly where internet connectivity, smartphone ownership and data affordability can limit access to digital platforms. The value of radio lay in its reliability, familiarity and local relevance. Using local announcers created an opportunity to communicate in familiar voices and languages and to connect messages to the community’s existing information networks. Radio also allowed the intervention to move beyond one-way messaging through interactive discussions and phone-in programmes.

Text messaging provided another layer of reinforcement. Rather than expecting farmers to remember everything from a single programme, text messages could reinforce key behaviours afterwards while reminding them about upcoming episodes.

The lesson for me was that “low-tech” should not be confused with “low-value.” The most appropriate technology is the one that fits people’s realities, routines and accesses and leverages trusted communication channels.  At the same time, this does not mean that radio and text messaging are the communication channels we need to use to reach everyone. Urban farmers and other populations with greater smartphone access may benefit from different Mobile Health approaches, including mobile applications, WhatsApp-based interventions, digital decision support tools, or more interactive platforms. The question should therefore not be “What technology is newest?” but “What technology fits the people, context and behaviour we are trying to influence?”

Perhaps the most important contribution of Human-Centred Design was that it helped me to move from focusing on which intervention I should deliver, to first understanding how the community wanted to be reached. Through co-design, farmers helped identify the importance of making the radio intervention engaging, familiar and locally relevant. This contributed to the decision to use a drama series, supported by text messages and locally familiar forms of storytelling and engagement, including kuyabila - a traditional poetic chanting or poetry used for local engagement and storytelling.

The drama format created an opportunity to place antimicrobial stewardship within everyday situations rather than presenting it only as technical information. Farmers could encounter characters, dilemmas and consequences that reflected experiences familiar to their own lives.

The use of kuyabila similarly provided an opportunity to draw on a locally meaningful form of expression and engagement, making the intervention feel less like an externally imposed health message and more connected to the community’s own ways of communicating.

Perhaps the most rewarding part of sharing this One Health experience at the UNICEF event was seeing how readily the lessons resonated with people working far beyond antimicrobial stewardship and outside animal health.

Lessons from dairy farmers can inform other sectors. The sectors may differ, but the behavioural questions remain similar: Have we listened? Do we understand the context? And have communities had a meaningful role in shaping the solution?
When we listen first, lessons travel far – and we design better.

title: Choosing a new management information system (MIS) - here's what you need to know before you buy
authors: Emma Bagley, MIS Commercial Lead, Department for Education

content.content: A new Department for Education (DfE) framework for buying a cloud-based management information system (MIS) is launching in September 2027. Ahead of this, there are steps you should take now depending on when your current contract ends.
This is a summary of the key actions that will help you stay compliant and avoid being locked into arrangements that delay your move to the new framework:
If your contracts expire shortly after launch, check whether there is enough time to use the framework and, if changing systems, complete the transition safely.
Why this matters to trusts now

The department is working towards the provision of a new MIS framework, due to be available in September 2027. The framework is designed not only to support compliance, but also to provide schools and trusts with greater transparency over costs, fairer contractual arrangements, clearer routes for resolving disputes, and improved protection from supplier lock-in.

Once it's live, you will be expected to use it for MIS procurement, rather than procuring directly from suppliers or via an alternative framework. This is to ensure that you benefit from the sector-specific terms and conditions.

The framework has been developed through extensive engagement with schools, trusts and suppliers since late 2025, including a sector working group established in February 2026. Feedback continues to shape the final framework requirements.

The framework is also designed to support a healthy and competitive market. It will reopen annually, allowing new suppliers to apply and existing suppliers to refresh their offers. This means schools and trusts will continue to benefit from innovation and choice, while gaining stronger contractual protections.

From 1 October 2026, the Academy Trust Handbook (para 2.30) states that trusts must ensure that all MIS contracts are aligned with DfE’s MIS framework by September 2027. More details about your contract management are available in the section below.

Where an existing MIS contract extends past September 2027, trusts are able to continue with that contract until it expires but should not exercise any available extension options. This ensures trusts benefit from the added protections offered by the framework.

If a trust does not comply, it will need to be able to explain why, for example insufficient network connectivity to host a cloud solution. Achieving better commercial rates will not be a valid exemption, as the framework is designed to deliver a wider range of benefits rather than be limited to cost savings. There is no reason why a supplier should charge you more for supplying via the DfE framework when compared to another route.
Why this matters to local authority-maintained schools

Local-authority-maintained schools are still expected to use the framework and follow the guidance in order to access the same value-for-money and protections that trusts will benefit from. However, as local authority-maintained schools are not covered by the Academy Trust Handbook, it is not a mandatory requirement for you.
Using the framework will also be in line with the communication issued on 8 June 2026 by the then Secretary of State for Education, Bridget Phillipson.
What you need to do with your existing MIS contract

Check when your current MIS contract ends, and act accordingly. If you have already started a compliant procurement exercise, you do not need to stop or restart it because of the forthcoming framework. If you're unsure, contact the department for advice or review one of the "Power Hour" recordings.

Scenario A: If your contract expires before 1 September 2027, extend it or replace it for a maximum of 12 months. Treat this as a transitional arrangement, bridging the gap until you can procure through the DfE framework.

Scenario B: If your supplier won't offer a 12-month extension, you'll need to re-procure instead. In this case, avoid signing a contract that runs for more than 3 years, including any extensions, so you're able to move to the DfE framework at your next renewal point. You should also look to seek agreement from the supplier and/or include in your procurement and contract documents the Core Principles, covered in section 3.

Scenario C: If your contract runs beyond 1 September 2027, don't use extension options that would delay your transition to the framework. When an academy trust awards its next full-term MIS contract, you must use the DfE MIS framework.

Scenario D: Your setting does not have sufficient network connectivity to host a cloud-based MIS and therefore needs to procure a MIS hosted by an ‘on-premises’ server. In this scenario, it is still advised that you seek the supplier’s agreement to the Core Principles (covered in section 3), and/or include them in your procurement and contract documents.
The Core Principles for interim procurement
If you fall into Scenario A, B or D above, and need to run any procurement activity before the framework launches, you should build specific safeguards into your tender documents.

Until the DfE framework launches, some schools and trusts will still need to procure or extend an MIS contract. If this applies to you, the guidance requires you to build the Core Principles into your tender documents and obtain supplier confirmation in writing.
Ask every potential supplier to do three things to avoid confusion later:
Speak to your data protection officer as part of this process since data protection is a key part of any MIS decision. The procuring EdTech guidance has more detail.
Staying on track and getting help
This is a multi-year transition with a national deadline.

Between now and launch, we'll keep engaging with schools, trusts and suppliers through webinars, sector events and published guidance. The questions you raise through these channels will directly shape our supporting materials and frequently asked questions (FAQs) ahead of implementation.
Expect regular updates as we move towards the September 2027 launch, including FAQs, practical guidance, "Power Hours", and answers to the questions schools and trusts are asking us.
Don't miss key information on the framework, implementation timelines and procurement guidance. Subscribe to the Maximising Value for Pupils newsletter, and follow us on LinkedIn and GOV.UK.
Your questions answered

We know schools and trusts will have questions about what the new MIS framework means in practice. We will be publishing some of your frequently asked questions soon. Sign up for notifications when this page is updated to stay informed.
